best_for: Windows and Linux users who watch a lot of local video and want a free player that remembers where they stopped in every file.
description:
SMPlayer is a desktop media player made by Ricardo Villalba. It plays video and audio files, and its interface is available in more than 30 languages.

Beyond plain playback, you can speed a video up or slow it down, fix audio or subtitles that run ahead of or behind the picture, and adjust the picture with the video equalizer. There are video and audio filters for further changes. You can send what you are watching to a TV with Chromecast, and on a 2-in-1 laptop with a touch screen you can control the player with your fingers.

points.title: Picks up where you left off
points.text: It remembers the position and settings of each file, such as audio track, subtitles and volume, so a long film or a series resumes exactly as you left it.

points.title: No codec packs
points.text: It is a front end for MPlayer and also works with mpv, which bring their own codecs. Most audio and video formats play without installing anything else.

points.title: Subtitles and YouTube
points.text: It can search for and download subtitles from opensubtitles.org, and play YouTube videos, with an optional plugin for YouTube search.

points.title: Free and GPL
points.text: SMPlayer is free and open source under the GPL. The site also offers skins and icon themes to change its look.

points.title: Windows gets the newest build
points.text: Windows is at 26.8.29, while the Mac and Linux builds listed here are at 25.6.0. The 64-bit installer needs Windows 8 or later; a separate unsigned 32-bit package covers Windows XP, and SmartScreen may warn before the installer runs.

points.title: Mac is the weak spot
points.text: Homebrew disabled its SMPlayer cask on 2026-09-01 because it fails Apple's Gatekeeper check, so expect macOS to block the app until you allow it by hand.

points.title: Linux Flatpak is official
points.text: The Flathub build is verified as published by the developer and runs on x64 and Arm64. The Windows listing keeps 10 versions; macOS and Linux list only the current release.
